newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada auto strike spreads, other industries hurt.
newsitem.headline: Canada auto strike spreads, other industries hurt.

text.p: (Dollars U.S. unless noted)
By Paul Casciato

As the strike at General Motors Corp. in Canada ended its fifth day Monday with no agreement in sight, the walkout was starting to affect GM plants in the United States and hundreds of small parts suppliers.

More than 15,000 members of the Canadian Auto Workers union went on strike last week in a dispute over the use of outside, non-union contractors, and another 6,000 workers joined the strike on Sunday.
By Wednesday, if no agreement is reached, all 26,000 hourly workers in Canada will be on strike and GM's plants will be idle.

GM plants in the United States and parts makers in both countries were already feeling the effects of the walkout Monday. The companies typically keep inventories of parts and other components low under the "just-in-time" delivery system.
"Everybody who supplies parts to an assembly plant that gets shut down is shut down themselves," said Dave Healy, analyst at Burnham Securities Inc.
Healy cited a similar impact last March when the United Auto Workers union struck two GM parts plants in Dayton, Ohio, and effectively shut down GM in North America for 17 days.
CAW President Buzz Hargrove told reporters Monday that the union's escalating strike strategy was meant to lessen the impact of the walkout on suppliers and give the company a chance to settle.
Negotiations have faltered on the issue of outsourcing -- the use of outside, usually non-union workers -- as well as hours and work rule issues.

"The real hit started last night with the shutting down of St. Catharines and Wednesday night of this week shutting down trim and transmission (plants in Windsor, Ontario)," Hargrove said. "A lot of those are where the U.S. (GM and parts) plants are going to lose production."

In the United States, GM said it idled 1,050 workers at its North Tonawanda, N.Y., engine plant that builds V-6 engines and told 800 workers at its Ypsilanti, Mich., transmission plant not to report to work on Tuesday.
Both facilities were only partly affected, a GM official said. North Tonawanda has 4,216 hourly workers, while Ypsilanti has 5,692.

The plants were hit by the halt of production of GM's popular Chevrolet Lumina sedans at the strike-bound Oshawa, Ontario, assembly complex. The Lumina uses North Tonawanda's 3.1-liter V-6 and Ypsilanti's front-drive transmissions.
GM has also had to halt production of its Camaro, Firebird, Buick Regal and Monte Carlo vehicles, as well as some trucks, at its Canadian plants.
In addition to the spread to GM's U.S. plants, hundreds if not thousands of smaller suppliers to GM stand to lose business.

Jason Myers, chief economist for the Alliance for Manufacturers and Exporters of Canada, told Maclean's magazine that a long strike would spill over to the steel, plastics, aluminum and leather industries in Canada.

A prolonged strike at GM Canada could hurt Canada's fledgling economic recovery and shave up to one point off fourth-quarter growth, government officials and analysts said Thursday, the first full day of the walkout.
Hargrove said he talked with GM's lead negotiator Dean Munger Monday but that the meeting deteriorated into a shouting match.
He said the union could decide to switch its lead bargaining team over to Ford Motor Co. if Wednesday passes without progress at the bargaining table with GM.
The St. Catharines, Ontario, plants idled on Sunday supply a wide range of components to GM's U.S. assembly plants, including V-6 and V-8 engines, truck axles, drive shafts and brake parts.
The strike started at GM's Oshawa plant hours before midnight on Wednesday.
